answers.text: Fixed three-line format every time — drop-off time, pallet count, damage noted — filled from the driver's message, not composed freely. A missing field still gets a line marked 'not stated'. It repeats because there's no wording decision to make, only slots to fill — the first thing I'd check if a rerun ever disagreed.

Split the week's calls into 'Needs follow-up' and 'No action needed', keeping time, customer, topic, outcome per line, with the count just the size of the first list. Entries that look like the same call logged twice get a note to check.
8am plus roughly six hours finishes early-to-mid afternoon on the 22nd itself, not the 23rd as the note says. I'd check the crew's actual sign-off time before filing it.

96 to 118 invoices is closer to 23% than the 20% quoted — that's off. The €58,000 balance split evenly is fine arithmetically, but nobody explains why it would sit flat the same month invoices jumped that much.
Output 2 — it shows 940 and 827 behind the 88%, so it can be checked. Output 1 gives no way to confirm the number without rerunning it.

Email 2 — it backs the ask with real numbers, 1,200 to 1,650 units from our own PO log, so the tier-2 claim can be checked. Email 1's 'better rate' has no numbers behind it. Before sending Email 1 I'd pull the real volumes from the PO log first.

Vendor pricing: no. Procurement spend: fine, it's a total. Next year's budget draft: no, unreleased. The vendor's published datasheet: yes. An employee's home address: no. Mostly it's about personal or not-yet-public.

Hourly rates and the retainer cap get redacted before anything goes into an unvetted tool. The non-disclosure clause names both the client and us, so that stays out too. The service scope itself is low-risk to paste as it stands. For the rates, I'd describe them in general terms rather than paste the figures in.

Before the reconciliation goes out, I cross-cast the closing stock figures against the warehouse system myself, as the last step. That catches a wrong total or a fabricated line, not just a typo. If it doesn't match, I hold it and flag my manager rather than send it up.

Step 1 is where a misread line item first enters the system. Step 4 is the one I'd actually gate, since that's where the approval note sends automatically if the match is within tolerance. I'd flag anything right at the edge of the tolerance band, or a line item missing from the original PO.
